question: How did an iron factory vessel in Scotland give painters one of their strongest modern blues?
answer: By contaminating a batch. In 1928 chemists at Scottish Dyes in Grangemouth found a stable blue-green impurity in phthalimide made in an iron vessel. The iron had joined the reaction. The compound, named phthalocyanine, was launched by ICI in 1935 as Monastral Blue. A reject batch became a staple of every artists' paint range.
move: Before throwing out a contaminated batch, ask what the contamination made.
reference: Frank H. Moser and Arthur L. Thomas, Phthalocyanine Compounds, Reinhold, 1963
